bull.argument: Alphabet's filing points to a durable, cash-generating franchise with multiple growth engines. Online advertising is still the core, yet the company reports that it generated more than 70% of total revenues from online advertising in 2025, meaning roughly 30% now comes from other sources. The filing says revenues from cloud, consumer subscriptions, platforms, and devices 'have grown over time' and that 'certain of these revenues have been growing at a rate higher than our advertising revenues.' Management also describes AI as a driver: user engagement with AI products 'will continue to benefit our business and our revenues.' The filing acknowledges heavy spending, with capital expenditures expected to 'significantly increase' in 2026, and lower margins on new revenue lines. Still, the company frames these as investments in its own infrastructure, including custom TPUs, that it expects to lower costs through efficiencies. Risks are real, but the filing shows a diversifying revenue base and a company actively building for the AI shift.

claims.claim: Advertising is still the majority of revenue, but the share is not total.
claims.quote: We generated more than 70% of total revenues from online advertising in 2025.

claims.claim: Non-advertising revenues are growing faster than advertising.
claims.quote: Certain of these revenues have been growing at a rate higher than our advertising revenues, becoming a larger percentage of our consolidated revenues, and we expect this trend to continue.

claims.claim: Management expects AI user engagement to benefit revenues and that efficiencies will offset infrastructure costs.
claims.quote: We expect that this evolution, including user engagement with AI products and services, will continue to benefit our business and our revenues.

bear.argument: The filing paints a company whose future rests on heavy, uncertain bets. Over 70% of 2025 revenue still came from online advertising, and the filing warns that AI 'is quickly reshaping the advertising industry' and that 'There is no assurance that we will adapt effectively.' Capital spending is set to 'significantly increase' in 2026, and the company says the resulting infrastructure costs are 'expected to significantly increase.' Those costs are partly fixed: 'Certain of our costs and expenses are relatively fixed and may not correlate to changes in revenue.' Management also warns of 'downward pressure on our operating margin,' and says the non-advertising lines that your opponent cites carry margins that 'are generally lower than the margins on our advertising revenues.' Growth from those lines therefore dilutes profitability. Finally, the company has taken on obligations: it provided 'credit support, such as through backstops and guarantees, to certain infrastructure related counterparties' and expects to keep using debt and finance leases. Diversification is real, but the filing shows rising capital needs, lower-margin growth, and contingent liabilities, which together make the stock a risky holding.

claims.claim: Advertising remains the dominant revenue source, leaving the company exposed to AI-driven shifts in ad delivery.
claims.quote: We generated more than 70% of total revenues from online advertising in 2025.

claims.claim: Management concedes it may not adapt effectively to AI reshaping advertising.
claims.quote: There is no assurance that we will adapt effectively and competitively to meet this shift

claims.claim: Non-advertising revenue lines carry lower margins, so their growth dilutes profitability.
claims.quote: The margins on these revenues vary significantly and are generally lower than the margins on our advertising revenues.

bull.argument: The bear case is serious, but it treats cost growth as if it were only a drag. The filing ties the 2026 capital build to demand: the company says developing and serving AI 'require more compute power than our historical consumer and enterprise offerings,' which is the reason infrastructure costs rise. Heavy spending is not the same as wasted spending, and the filing gives reasons to expect returns, including growth in cloud, subscriptions, platforms, and devices that is 'growing at a rate higher than our advertising revenues.' On margins, the filing does say lower-margin lines dilute profitability, but it also says the company expects to 'continue to drive efficiencies in our data centers, for example, through the design of our AI models and our TPU and GPU-based technical infrastructure.' On credit support and debt, the filing describes these as tools used to fund infrastructure, not signs of distress; it reports no default. The filing does name real risks, and an investor should size the position accordingly. But the company is funding a shift in its core business from a position of more than 70% advertising and growing diversified revenues.

claims.claim: Management ties rising infrastructure costs to AI demand requiring more compute.
claims.quote: developing and serving AI offerings require more compute power than our historical consumer and enterprise offerings.

claims.claim: Non-advertising revenues are growing faster than advertising revenues.
claims.quote: Certain of these revenues have been growing at a rate higher than our advertising revenues

claims.claim: The company expects efficiencies in data centers from its own AI and TPU designs.
claims.quote: we expect to continue to drive efficiencies in our data centers, for example, through the design of our AI models and our TPU and GPU-based technical infrastructure.

bear.argument: The opponent's case rests on expectations, not results. The filing says the AI build 'require[s] more compute power' and that costs are 'expected to significantly increase,' but it offers no return figures, and it concedes that investments 'ultimately may not be commercially viable or may not result in an adequate return of capital.' The efficiency claim is also a forecast: management says it 'expect[s] to continue to drive efficiencies,' while separately warning that 'we may also not be able to continue to drive efficiencies at the rate we have in the past.' The growth of non-advertising lines does not rescue margins; the filing says those revenues are 'generally lower than the margins on our advertising revenues,' so faster growth there mechanically dilutes the mix. On financing, the absence of default is not the test. The filing states the company 'provided credit support, such as through backstops and guarantees, to certain infrastructure related counterparties' and 'may continue to provide additional credit support,' which are contingent obligations that could become real if counterparties fail. Concentrated spending, falling-margin growth, and open-ended guarantees make a risky position, regardless of today's cash flow.

claims.claim: Management admits AI investments may not earn an adequate return.
claims.quote: Our investments ultimately may not be commercially viable or may not result in an adequate return of capital

claims.claim: Management warns it may not keep up the efficiency gains it has achieved before.
claims.quote: we may also not be able to continue to drive efficiencies at the rate we have in the past

claims.claim: The company has provided guarantees that create contingent exposure to infrastructure counterparties.
claims.quote: we provided credit support, such as through backstops and guarantees, to certain infrastructure related counterparties

judge.reasoning: All quotes in both sides are verified, but the bear side draws on more pointed, verified risk language (no assurance of adaptation, non-viable investment admission, guarantees) and directly rebuts the bull's efficiency and growth claims by showing they are forecasts and that lower-margin growth mechanically dilutes profitability. The bull's responses on guarantees and returns were thinner, relying on 'no default' as evidence and not directly addressing the admission that investments may not earn adequate returns.
